title: Learning Is Not Often What You Think It Is
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles challenges the most persistent misconception teachers hold about high-achieving classes: that their success is primarily a product of ability. His central argument, developed through a series of questions to teachers about their own experience, is that the most consistently predictive factor in academic success is not intelligence but effort and hard work — and that confusing the two has systematic consequences for how teachers design instruction, assign challenge, and interpret student failure. The article traces the mechanism: when teachers attribute high achievement to natural ability, they are less likely to believe that deliberate practice, struggle, and repeated retrieval can move less naturally able students — which becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. Salles draws on research on growth mindset, deliberate practice, and memory science to argue that what looks like ability in successful students is usually accumulated practice that has become automatized, creating the appearance of effortlessness that misleads observers into thinking the student didn't have to work. The article closes with direct implications for classroom practice: explicitly valuing effort over performance, designing tasks that require productive struggle rather than smooth execution, and building feedback cultures that treat errors as diagnostic information rather than evidence of fixed capacity.
points: The core insight is that automatized expertise looks like effortlessness to observers: when a high-achieving student appears to 'just get it,' what they are demonstrating is not natural ability but the result of accumulated practice that has been chunked and automatized — which observers (and the students themselves) then misattribute to innate capacity.

Attributing success to ability rather than effort has direct consequences for instructional design: teachers who believe their top students succeed because they're smart design for those students by giving them harder problems, while students who believe they succeed because they're smart avoid challenge that might reveal the attribution was wrong — a double failure mode.

Growth mindset research is the article's evidentiary foundation: Dweck's decades of research demonstrate that the belief that intelligence is fixed versus growable is itself one of the most powerful predictors of persistence, challenge-seeking, and recovery from failure — independent of actual ability level.

The practical classroom implication is about feedback design: praising effort and strategy rather than outcomes or ability changes the signal students receive about what is within their control, and this change in perceived locus of control is consistently associated with improved persistence on hard tasks.

The article's most useful reframe for teachers is about what to make of lazy high-achievers: a student who succeeds without visible effort is not demonstrating that effort is unnecessary — they are demonstrating what invisible prior effort looks like when it has become automated, which should prompt teachers to ask 'what did this student do to get here?' rather than 'why can't other students just do what this student does?'
